newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank derivatives activity hits record Q2 - OCC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank derivatives activity hits record Q2 - OCC.

text.p: Derivatives activity by U.S. commercial banks hit record levels in the second quarter of 1996, according to a report by the Comptroller of the Currency Administrator of National Banks (OCC) in Washington, D.C.

The notional amount of derivatives in commercial bank portfolios rose to $19 trillion in the second quarter of 1996, an increase of $1.2 trillion over the previous quarter, the OCC said. Derivatives activity by U.S. banks has more than doubled since the end of 1992, when it stood at $8.8 trillion.
The $19 trillion figure excludes spot foreign exchange contracts, which dropped $2.5 billion to $560 billion.

The number of U.S. banks holding derivatives decreased by 42 in the second quarter to 507. However, among the nine banks that dominate the U.S. derivatives markets, the average percentage of credit exposure to risk based capital rose to 244.1 percent from 233.7, the report said.
The nine banks account for 94 percent of the total notional amount of derivatives in the banking system.

The notional amounts of interest rate derivatives rose $698 billion to $12.52 trillion while foreign exchange activity rose $476 billion to $6.1 trillion. Together, the two account for 98 percent of all derivatives activity worldwide.
Commodity and equity contracts in bank portfolios increased by $16 billion to $394 billion, the report said.

Trading revenue dropped by $62 million to $1.9 billion in the second quarter. The top nine banks realized 86 percent of that revenue. A third of the revenue was seen by Morgan Guaranty Trust, which realized $634 million, it said.
Eighty-six percent of the contracts were traded in the over-the-counter market, and 14 percent via exchanges.
